guide.summary: Unit 3 covers how data are produced and what conclusions they support: observational studies vs. experiments, sampling methods and their biases, and the principles of experimental design (comparison, random assignment, control, replication, blocking). The scope of inference (generalization vs. causation) is tested on nearly every exam.

sections.heading: Studies and scope of inference
sections.body: In an observational study, researchers measure variables without imposing treatments; it can show association but not causation because of possible confounding variables. In an experiment, researchers deliberately impose treatments. Scope of inference: random sampling from a population allows generalizing results to that population; random assignment of treatments allows cause-and-effect conclusions. A study can have one, both, or neither.

sections.heading: Sampling methods
sections.body: Simple random sample (SRS): every group of n individuals has an equal chance; use a random number generator or numbered slips. Stratified random sample: divide the population into homogeneous strata (e.g., grade level) and take an SRS from each; it reduces variability of estimates when the stratifying variable is related to the response. Cluster sample: divide into heterogeneous clusters (e.g., classrooms) and randomly select entire clusters; it is cheaper and easier. Systematic random sample: choose a random start, then every kth individual. Convenience and voluntary response samples are biased.

sections.heading: Sources of bias
sections.body: Bias is a systematic tendency to over- or underestimate. Undercoverage: some groups are left out of the sampling frame (e.g., a phone survey missing people without phones). Nonresponse: selected individuals don't respond. Response bias: answers are inaccurate because of question wording, interviewer influence, or sensitive topics. Voluntary response: people with strong opinions choose to participate. To earn full credit, explain the direction of the bias: which group is over- or underrepresented, and why the estimate is likely too high or too low. Larger samples reduce variability but do not fix bias.

sections.heading: Experimental design
sections.body: Components: experimental units (or subjects), treatments, explanatory and response variables. Principles: comparison of two or more treatments (often including a control group or placebo), random assignment to create roughly equivalent groups, control of other variables, and replication (enough units per treatment). Blinding (single or double) reduces bias from expectations; placebos address the placebo effect. Designs: completely randomized; randomized block (split units into blocks that are similar on a variable likely to affect the response, then randomly assign treatments within each block, which reduces variability); matched pairs (each subject receives both treatments in random order, or similar pairs are split). A result is statistically significant when it is unlikely to occur by chance alone from random assignment.

sections.heading: Worked example: designing an experiment
sections.body: To test whether a new fertilizer increases tomato yield, a researcher has 40 plants. A completely randomized design assigns 20 plants at random to the new fertilizer and 20 to the standard fertilizer, perhaps by numbering plants 1–40 and using a random number generator to select 20. If plants differ in sunlight exposure, a randomized block design groups plants by location and randomizes treatments within each block, reducing variability. The response variable is yield in pounds, and comparing average yields lets the researcher conclude whether the fertilizer causes a difference.

sections.heading: Scope of inference
sections.body: Random sampling allows generalization to the population sampled; random assignment allows cause-and-effect conclusions. A study with both supports causal conclusions about the population. An observational study cannot establish causation because of possible confounding variables, even if it uses a random sample.

sections.heading: Sources of bias in practice
sections.body: Undercoverage occurs when some groups are left out of the sampling frame, such as households without phones. Nonresponse occurs when selected individuals do not respond. Response bias arises from question wording or interviewer effects. Voluntary response and convenience samples typically overrepresent people with strong opinions or easy access.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students confuse random sampling with random assignment, describe randomization vaguely, and forget to name the response variable and treatments.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know population, sample, census, simple random sample, stratified and cluster samples, bias, observational study, experiment, confounding, control group, placebo, blinding, blocking, and matched pairs.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: Experimental design questions ask you to describe a randomization method in enough detail that someone could carry it out, explain the purpose of a control group or blocking, and identify the scope of inference.

keyTakeaways: Random sampling → generalize; random assignment → causation.
Strata are homogeneous; clusters are heterogeneous.
Explain bias direction: who is missing and how it shifts the estimate.
Blocking reduces variability from a known source.
commonMistakes: Saying random assignment allows generalizing to a population.
Describing randomization without explaining how (e.g., 'randomly assign' with no method).
Blocking on a variable unrelated to the response.
Naming a bias without stating its direction.
examTips: Experimental design FRQs require a complete, replicable randomization method.
When asked why block, say the blocking variable affects the response, so blocking reduces variability in the comparison.
For bias, identify the specific group and the direction of the error.
For scope of inference, address both random sampling and random assignment.
guide.cramSheet:
**Scope:** random sample → population · random assignment → cause

**Sampling:** SRS · stratified (similar within, SRS each) · cluster (whole groups) · systematic (every kth)

**Bias:** undercoverage · nonresponse · response (wording) · voluntary · convenience · state direction

**Experiment:** compare · randomly assign · control · replicate

**Designs:** completely randomized · block (similar units) · matched pairs

**Blinding:** single/double · placebo effect

vocab.definition: A study that observes individuals and measures variables without imposing treatments.
A study that deliberately imposes treatments on individuals to measure responses.
When two variables' effects on a response cannot be distinguished.
A sample in which every group of n individuals has an equal chance to be selected.
Separate SRSs from each of several homogeneous groups (strata).
A sample formed by randomly selecting entire groups (clusters).
Bias when some members of the population are less likely to be included in the sample.
Bias when selected individuals cannot be contacted or refuse to participate.
Bias when responses are systematically inaccurate due to wording, interviewer, or sensitivity.
Using a chance process to assign experimental units to treatments.
Units grouped into blocks of similar units, with random assignment of treatments within each block.
A design comparing two treatments within pairs of similar units or within each subject.

practice.stem: Researchers review medical records and find that people who drink green tea daily have lower blood pressure. This is

choices.text: an experiment, so green tea lowers blood pressure
an observational study, so a cause-and-effect conclusion is not justified
a census, so the results apply to everyone
a matched pairs experiment

practice.explanation: No treatment was imposed; tea drinkers may differ in diet, exercise, or other factors.

practice.stem: A school selects 4 of its 40 homerooms at random and surveys every student in those homerooms. This is a

choices.text: stratified random sample
systematic random sample
cluster sample
convenience sample

distractors.A: Would sample some students from every homeroom.

practice.stem: A radio host asks listeners to call in and say whether they support a new tax. Most callers oppose it. The main problem is

choices.text: random assignment was not used
the sample is too large
stratification by station
voluntary response bias, because people with strong opinions are more likely to call

practice.explanation: Self-selected respondents overrepresent strong (often negative) opinions.

practice.stem: In an experiment, the main purpose of random assignment of subjects to treatments is to

choices.text: create treatment groups that are roughly equivalent, so differences in response can be attributed to the treatments
allow results to be generalized to a larger population
eliminate the placebo effect
increase the sample size

practice.explanation: Randomization balances the effects of other variables across groups on average.

practice.stem: To estimate average weekly hours of exercise among adults in a city, researchers survey people leaving a downtown gym at 6 p.m. The estimate is most likely

choices.text: too low, because people are tired after exercising
too high, because people at a gym exercise more than typical adults
unbiased, because the sample is random
unbiased if the sample size is large enough

practice.explanation: The convenience sample overrepresents frequent exercisers.

practice.stem: A university wants to estimate average student debt. Debt levels differ greatly between undergraduates and graduate students. Which design gives the most precise estimate for a fixed sample size?

choices.text: An SRS of all students
A cluster sample of dormitories
A stratified random sample with undergraduates and graduate students as strata
A sample of students who respond to an email

practice.explanation: Stratifying on a variable related to the response reduces variability of the estimate.

distractors.B: Dorms are heterogeneous and may exclude graduate students.

practice.stem: In a study of a new pain reliever, neither the patients nor the doctors evaluating their pain know which patients received the drug and which received a placebo. This is done to

choices.text: prevent expectations of patients and evaluators from influencing the results
increase the sample size
ensure random sampling
create blocks

practice.explanation: Double blinding reduces bias from the placebo effect and from evaluators' expectations.

practice.stem: A researcher tests two sunscreens. Each of 30 volunteers applies sunscreen A to one forearm and B to the other, with the arm chosen by a coin flip. This design is

choices.text: completely randomized
a cluster sample
an observational study
matched pairs

practice.explanation: Each subject receives both treatments, with random assignment of arms.

practice.stem: Volunteers from a single gym are randomly assigned to two diets, and Diet A produces significantly greater weight loss. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: Diet A causes greater weight loss for all adults.
No cause-and-effect conclusion is possible.
Diet A causes greater weight loss for volunteers like those in the study, but results may not generalize to all adults.
The results apply to all gym members nationwide.

practice.explanation: Random assignment supports causation; lack of random sampling limits generalization.

practice.stem: A survey asks, "Do you agree that the city should stop wasting money on its failing bus system?" The question is likely to produce

choices.text: response bias from loaded wording that pushes respondents toward agreement
undercoverage
nonresponse bias
no bias, because the question is clear

practice.explanation: 'Wasting' and 'failing' lead respondents toward one answer.

practice.stem: An agronomist compares two fertilizers on 20 plots. Ten plots are on a hillside with poor soil and ten are in a fertile valley. Which design is best, and why?

choices.text: Completely randomized, because randomization handles everything
Use only the valley plots to avoid variability
Put fertilizer A on the hillside and B in the valley
Block by location and randomly assign each fertilizer to 5 plots within each block, because soil quality affects yield and blocking removes that source of variability from the comparison

practice.explanation: Blocking on a variable that affects the response makes treatment differences easier to detect.

practice.stem: A random sample of 2,000 households is selected from a landline telephone directory to estimate the proportion of adults under 30 who rent their homes. Which is the most serious problem?

choices.text: The sample is too small
Undercoverage: younger adults, who are more likely to rent, are less likely to have landlines, so the proportion would likely be underestimated
Response bias from question wording
The estimate will be unbiased because the sample is random

practice.explanation: The sampling frame systematically excludes the group of interest, and the bias has a predictable direction.

distractors.D: Random selection from a flawed frame is still biased.

practice.stem: A study finds that students who take music lessons have higher math grades. A school wants to conclude that music lessons improve math. Which is the best design to test this?

choices.text: Randomly assign volunteer students to receive music lessons or a comparable non-music activity, then compare math grade changes
Compare math grades of students who choose to take lessons with those who don't
Survey parents about whether music helps math
Take a census of all students' grades

practice.explanation: Random assignment with a comparison activity controls for confounders such as family income and motivation.

practice.stem: In a randomized experiment, the difference in mean recovery time between a treatment and control group is 'statistically significant.' This means

choices.text: the difference is large enough to be important to patients
the treatment works for every patient
a difference this large would be unlikely to occur by chance alone from random assignment if the treatment had no effect
the results can be generalized to all patients

practice.explanation: Statistical significance is about chance variation, not practical importance or generalization.

practice.prompt: A company has developed a new app intended to improve sleep quality. Researchers recruit 80 adult volunteers: 40 who work night shifts and 40 who work day shifts. Each volunteer will use either the new app or a standard relaxation-audio app for four weeks, and sleep quality will be measured on a 0–100 scale.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the treatments and the response variable.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe how to carry out a randomized block design for this study, including how treatments are assigned.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why blocking by shift type is beneficial.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: If the new app performs significantly better, to what population can the result be generalized? Explain.

rubric.description: Treatments: new sleep app and standard relaxation app. Response: sleep quality score after 4 weeks.

Blocks by shift (night/day). Within each block, number the 40 volunteers 1–40, use a random number generator to select 20 distinct numbers for the new app; the other 20 get the standard app. Compare results within blocks.
Shift type likely affects sleep quality (night workers likely sleep worse); blocking accounts for this source of variability, making it easier to detect a difference between apps.
Cause-and-effect can be concluded (random assignment), but only for volunteers similar to these, since they were not randomly sampled from a larger population.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) The treatments are the new sleep app and the standard relaxation-audio app. The response variable is the volunteer's sleep quality score (0–100) at the end of four weeks.

(b) Separate the volunteers into two blocks: 40 night-shift workers and 40 day-shift workers. Within the night-shift block, assign each volunteer a number from 1 to 40. Use a random number generator to select 20 different numbers; those volunteers use the new app, and the remaining 20 use the standard app. Repeat independently in the day-shift block. After four weeks, compare mean sleep quality scores for the two apps within each block, then combine the comparisons.

(c) Shift type is likely to affect sleep quality, since night-shift workers sleep against their natural rhythms. Blocking ensures each app is tested equally in both groups and removes variation due to shift type from the comparison, making a real difference between the apps easier to detect.

(d) Because volunteers were randomly assigned to apps, we could conclude the new app causes better sleep quality. However, they were volunteers, not a random sample, so the result can only be generalized to adults similar to these volunteers.
